answers.l: Ron Rivest, 1991. Practical collisions came in 2004. The Flame malware used one to forge a Microsoft signing certificate.
Part of SHA-2, published by NIST in 2001. Bitcoin hashes with it twice.
SHAttered, 2017: Google and CWI made two different PDFs with the same SHA-1. Git is moving to SHA-256.
Provos and Mazières, 1999, built on Blowfish. Its cost factor keeps it slow on purpose.
Faster than SHA-256 on 64-bit CPUs.
A checksum, not a cryptographic hash. In zip, PNG and Ethernet.
Keccak, standardized in 2015. A sponge construction, nothing like SHA-2 inside.
Fast and secure. Used inside Argon2 and WireGuard.
2020. A Merkle tree inside, so it spreads across cores.
Austin Appleby, 2008. Fast and non-cryptographic.
Yann Collet, who also wrote LZ4 and Zstandard.
Fowler, Noll and Vo. Multiply by a prime, XOR a byte, repeat.
Aumasson and Bernstein, 2012. Stops hash-flooding attacks. Python and Rust hash with it.
Won the Password Hashing Competition in 2015.
Colin Percival, 2009, for Tarsnap. Memory-hard, so GPUs don’t help much.
An HMAC iterated many times. NIST-approved, but GPU-friendly.
Rivest, 1990. Windows NTLM password hashes are still MD4.
Bitcoin addresses: SHA-256, then RIPEMD-160.
SHA-256, truncated, with different starting values.
SHA-512, truncated, which also resists length extension.
Google, 2011, for strings.
CityHash’s successor.
Daniel J. Bernstein: hash * 33 + c, starting from 5381.
Mark Adler, for zlib. Faster than CRC32 and weaker.
A one-time authenticator, paired with ChaCha20 in TLS and WireGuard.
Small and fast. Zig’s standard hash maps use it.
The tiny, fast hash rustc uses internally. It came from Firefox.
Position-aware sums, cheaper than CRC.
Rijmen and Barreto, 2000. Named after the Whirlpool Galaxy.
Anderson and Biham, 1995. Designed for 64-bit CPUs.
Rivest, 1989, for 8-bit machines.
Rivest’s SHA-3 entry, withdrawn before the second round.
A SHA-3 finalist from a team that included Bruce Schneier.
A SHA-3 finalist built from AES-like parts.
A SHA-3 finalist by Hongjun Wu.
Keccak with 12 rounds instead of 24.
Russia’s GOST hash standard.
China’s national hash standard.
1992. Variable rounds and variable output length.
Ralph Merkle, 1990. Named after an Egyptian pharaoh.
Peter Pearson, 1990. Hashes bytes through a 256-entry permutation table.
Bob Jenkins, released on Halloween 2011.
Bob Jenkins. Perl used it for years.
Google, 2016. Keyed hashing with SIMD.
The polynomial authenticator inside AES-GCM.
